## Historical audit: S0103

**Source:** `/srv/lab-disks/disk2/users/xymo/Documents/Codex/2026-11-02/scene-rsi-rsi-1-3d-blender/outputs/scene_rsi_pilot/results/r2/generic_rsi/C2/development/commons_118588033/trajectory.jsonl`. Citations below refer to JSONL lines in that file. No observations are split across supplied chunks.

**Goal versus interpretation.** The explicit task was to reconstruct an indoor photograph as an editable SceneAct/Blender hierarchy matching the viewpoint, objects and materials, without using the photograph as a texture. The student's “ship compartment” and object identifications are its visual interpretation, not independently verified facts (line 1, student model_request; line 3, student model_response).

| Evidence | Observed operation or result |
|---|---|
| Initial build | The student programmed multiple semantic assets: architecture, three-tier berths, cabinets, lockers, chair, pillar, bench, fixtures and lamps. Chair parts were grouped and rotated together; this is hierarchy and pose evidence, not proof of physical contact. Palette materials, roughness and localized copied materials were coded; no image texture or procedural surface pattern was used (lines 3–4, model_response and execute). |
| First validation | Step 1 executed successfully and saved a render; inventory reported 216 primitives (line 5, execution_result). The render and reference were supplied to the next student session (lines 7–8). The student reported ceiling/framing and anchor mismatches, edge-on fixtures and excessive brightness; these are student assessments, not independent visual findings (line 9). |
| Revision 2 | The executed rewrite moved the camera, changed lens and aim, added a partial bulkhead and foreground bench, reoriented fixtures, and reduced lighting/exposure. It also changed geometry and wall color, so effects are not isolated (lines 9–10). Step 2 rendered successfully, with 228 primitives (line 11, execution_result). |
| Revision 3 | After receiving both prior renders, the student judged the camera framing plausible but reported misplaced pillar, lamp and berth and a hidden board. The executed rewrite retained the camera, moved whole assets, added a doorway, darkened finishes and exposure, and asserted nonempty floor and emission targets (lines 13–16). Step 3 rendered successfully with 230 primitives (line 17). |
| Selection | With no executions remaining, the student was supplied all three renders and selected step 3; the controller recorded that selection (lines 19–22). Selection is not a fidelity score or independent geometric verification. |

**Teacher input and exploration.** No teacher event, teacher diagnosis or teacher-specific update appears in this student trajectory; consequently there is no evidence of teacher receipt or adoption. The shared system procedure and controller review requests were actual inputs, and the student visibly used anchor ledgers, render-based self-assessments and successive rewrites. Sessions recorded no tool calls; exploration was through the controller’s three executions, not independent filesystem or external-model investigation (lines 1–2, 7–8, 13–14, 19–20).

**Outcome and uncertainty.** This is a **formal execution success**, with three successful renders and a recorded final selection; visual correctness remains unknown, not established by logs or object names. The supplied observations contain image paths, not the image pixels for this audit. Thus actual object coverage, texture resemblance, occlusions, part contact, camera match, lighting and improvement across steps cannot be independently checked. In particular, whether the added partition and doorway match the photograph and whether moved supports intersect correctly remain hypotheses.

**Lessons:** The transferable pattern is to distinguish executable inventories and semantic grouping from visual and contact validation, and to track camera, geometry and appearance separately. The particular pillar, berth and brightness corrections are task-specific student hypotheses, not demonstrated general rules.
